# Incident Report: MTA-2024-08-15

## Victim host
| Field | Value | Evidence |
|---|---|---|
| IPv4 | 10.8.15.133 | DHCP lease, all subsequent traffic |
| MAC | 00:1c:bf:03:54:82 | ARP (`Who has 10.8.15.4? Tell 10.8.15.133`), confirmed as `eth.src` on every frame from 10.8.15.133 |
| Windows hostname | DESKTOP-H8ALZBV | DHCP option 12 (hostname), NBNS registration `DESKTOP-H8ALZBV<00>/<20>`, mDNS `DESKTOP-H8ALZBV.local` |
| AD domain | lafontainebleu.org (workgroup/NetBIOS alias LAFONTAINEBLEU) | NBNS, Kerberos realm, DNS SRV lookups for `_ldap._tcp...lafontainebleu.org` |
| Logged-in user | plucero | Kerberos `CNameString` in AS-REQ/TGS traffic between 10.8.15.133 and the domain controller 10.8.15.4 |

Domain controller: 10.8.15.4 (WIN-JEGJIX7Q9RS.lafontainebleu.org, MAC 64:00:6a:8c:9c:40). Gateway: 10.8.15.1 (MAC 00:16:9c:02:a7:4b).

## Malware family
**"Knock" loader/backdoor** — attribution is **behavioral, corroborated by an embedded debug artifact**, not a signature match (no IDS/Suricata export was present in the evidence directory).

- The second-stage payload pulled to disk is a PE32+ DLL (SHA256 below) that contains the embedded PDB debug path `E:\work\ooooooops\181\knock_v1.1.8\knock\bin64\knock.pdb`, an internal project name of "knock" — this is the strongest identifying artifact recovered.
- Behaviorally, the infection chain (oversized padded JS "invoice" downloader → LOLBin BITS transfer of a bare-hex-named DLL → persistent HTTP GET `/` beaconing with a spoofed obsolete IE6 user-agent string) is consistent with known invoice-themed JS-downloader-to-loader campaigns, but I did not have internet access or IDS signatures to cross-check the family name publicly, so treat "Knock" as the artifact-derived name rather than a confirmed public threat-actor label.

## Delivery chain (chronological, all timestamps relative to capture start)

1. **t≈74.7s** — Victim browses (real Edge 127 user-agent) to `http://quote.checkfedexexp.com/managements?...` (resolves to Cloudflare-fronted 104.21.55.70 / 172.67.170.159), a FedEx-themed phishing lure. Response is a 2.77 MB ZIP archive containing `Invoice-876597035-003-8331775-8334138.js` (6,990,020 bytes) — a JScript file padded with megabytes of scraped academic/PDF text (MPI standard docs, IPCC report text, etc.) to inflate its size past AV/sandbox limits. The script contains `WScript.Sleep` calls (Windows Script Host execution) and one embedded reference to `https://business.checkfedexexp.com/data-privacy?...` — the same C2 domain family.
2. **t≈101–127s** — Benign Windows Delivery Optimization / BITS traffic to `msedge.b.tlu.dl.delivery.mp.microsoft.com` (legitimate Microsoft update background noise, not malicious).
3. **t≈135.9s** — The malicious script triggers a **BITS job** (`Microsoft BITS/7.8` user-agent, a LOLBin technique to blend in with legitimate Windows update traffic) that HEADs then GETs `http://72.5.43.29/data/0f60a3e7baecf2748b1c8183ed37d1e4` — a PE32+ DLL, 159,232 bytes, no DNS lookup preceded this request (hardcoded IP).
4. **t≈196.9s onward** — The dropped DLL begins C2 beaconing: repeated `GET /` (and occasional `POST /`) to `72.5.43.29:80`, roughly every 5–10 seconds, continuing for the remainder of the capture (303 beacon requests observed spanning ~1930 seconds), all using the static, spoofed user-agent `Mozilla / 5.0 (compatible; MSIE 6.0; Windows NT 5.1; SV1; .NET CLR 1.0.3705)`.

## Indicators of Compromise

| Type | Value | Evidence |
|---|---|---|
| c2_endpoint | 72.5.43.29:80 | 303 beacon `GET /` + 3 `POST /` requests from victim, plus initial BITS payload fetch; contacted directly by IP with no preceding DNS query |
| domain | quote.checkfedexexp.com | HTTP GET `/managements?...` request, Host header, DNS A record → 104.21.55.70, 172.67.170.159 |
| domain | business.checkfedexexp.com | DNS A record → 172.67.170.159, 104.21.55.70; referenced inside the malicious JS payload |
| url | `http://quote.checkfedexexp.com/managements?16553a25e45250a41fd5&endeds=MIGpq&JStx=59bf050d37df88a9-ade43358-eaa1220b-0571422b-0f33e6aa150e86bafd0ed4&Ld=9d7502d88d752a27b1d00587309184b5a215` | Full HTTP request URI, frame 6418; response delivered the malicious ZIP/JS |
| url | `http://72.5.43.29/data/0f60a3e7baecf2748b1c8183ed37d1e4` | BITS HEAD/GET, frames 10611/10614 |
| file_name | Invoice-876597035-003-8331775-8334138.js | Filename inside ZIP retrieved from quote.checkfedexexp.com |
| file_hash | ZIP container: 798563fcf7600f7ef1a35996291a9dfb5f9902733404dd499e2e736ea1dc6fc5 (SHA256) | Reassembled from HTTP response body, frame 6418 stream |
| file_name | 0f60a3e7baecf2748b1c8183ed37d1e4 | BITS-delivered second-stage DLL (no file extension by design) |
| file_hash | b7aec5f73d2a6bbd8cd920edb4760e2edadc98c3a45bf4fa994d47ca9cbd02f6 (SHA256) | Computed from exported HTTP object (159,232 bytes, PE32+ DLL x86-64) |
| artifact | PDB path `E:\work\ooooooops\181\knock_v1.1.8\knock\bin64\knock.pdb` | Embedded string in the second-stage DLL — source of the "Knock" family name |

## Benign context (not indicators)
- Microsoft telemetry/CDN/update domains: `*.microsoft.com`, `*.msn.com`, `*.bing.com`, `*.msedge.net`, `*.azureedge.net`, `msedge.b.tlu.dl.delivery.mp.microsoft.com` (legit BITS/Delivery Optimization traffic for two Windows Update filestreamingservice IDs, `8f2381c2-...` and `f37dd878-...`).
- `acroipm2.adobe.com`, `armmf.adobe.com` — Adobe update/licensing checks.
- `oneocsp.microsoft.com` — OCSP certificate revocation check.
- `www.msftconnecttest.com` — Windows NCSI connectivity test.
- SSDP M-SEARCH broadcasts to 239.255.255.250:1900 from Microsoft Edge — normal device discovery.
- Internal AD/domain traffic: DHCP, NBNS, mDNS/LLMNR, CLDAP, Kerberos, LDAP, DCE/RPC to 10.8.15.4 — normal domain-join/logon chatter.

## Incident summary
The Windows workstation DESKTOP-H8ALZBV (10.8.15.133, MAC 00:1c:bf:03:54:82), logged on as user **plucero** in the lafontainebleu.org domain, was infected after browsing to a FedEx-themed phishing page at quote.checkfedexexp.com, which delivered a ZIP-wrapped, deliberately oversized JavaScript "invoice" downloader. That script abused BITSAdmin to retrieve a second-stage DLL (SHA256 b7aec5f73d2a6bbd8cd920edb4760e2edadc98c3a45bf4fa994d47ca9cbd02f6, internally named "knock" per its embedded PDB path) directly from IP 72.5.43.29, which then established persistent HTTP command-and-control beaconing to 72.5.43.29:80 using a spoofed, obsolete Internet Explorer 6 user-agent string that continued through the end of the capture.
